title: The Gotham Gambit
description: A tricky choice against 1.e4, this Petroff Gambit leads to attacking positions where you can crush your opponent.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/4N2q/3P4/2N4b/PPP1B.text:
This is White’s best move, but it’s a hard one to find. 

It’s a discovered attack on our queen and a strong defensive resource.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/4N3/3P3q/2N4b/PPP1B.text:
We shift the queen forward to stay active and keep up the pressure. 

Capturing the bishop would be a blunder. The best move for White now is 12.g3, which would force us to take on d4.

The position is +1.2 for White, but we equalize material, and the sequence of moves up to this point is not easy to find.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/6B1/8/2NP1N1q/PPP1B.text: White develops the bishop, but this only helps us, as it allows us to jump forward with the knight.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/3P2b1/2N2N1P/PPP.text:
This is White’s best option. They take space in the center, shut down any ...Nd4 ideas, and open up their dark-squared bishop.

But we sacrifice the bishop anyway! 

It’s not the best move, but a very interesting one. We want to open up the White king and induce a mistake.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/3P4/2N2N1P/PPP1B.text: If White accepts the sacrifice, it’s a blunder, and we’ve achieved our goal of tricking them into weakening their king.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6P1/2N2N2/PPPPBP.text:
White takes the bishop — but it is a blunder!

We recapture with the knight, which now also targets the vulnerable h2-square.

Ideas like ...Bh2+ and ...Rhe8 are exactly what we should be aiming for next.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2N4P/PPPPBPP.text:
White might be aiming to simplify by inviting trades, but it’s not the best option.

It leaves us with a slightly better position.

We go ahead and trade the light-squared bishops.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2NP1N1P/PPP1.text:
Here’s a cleaner version that reflects that intention:

Instead of capturing the bishop, White opens the diagonal for their dark-squared bishop. But this move is also losing.

We sacrifice the bishop anyway! The goal is simple: rip open the kingside and launch a mating attack.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2NP1NP1/PPP1.text:
White opens up their dark-squared bishop, which is now ready to be developed.

We bring the other rook into the game. Now all of our pieces are developed and active. 

We’re threatening ...Rxe2, which could win two pieces for a rook while also taking control of the light squares near White’s king.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/8/2N4P/PPPPQPPN/.text: If White recaptures with the queen...

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/8/2NP1N1P/PPP1BP.text:
White accepts the sacrifice, but they shouldn’t have done that. 

Their king is now exposed, and White is already nearly losing.

We recapture with the queen. The king now has no escape.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/8/7P/PPPPNPPN/R1.text: White could also recapture with the knight instead.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/8/3P4/2N2N1q/PPP1BP.text:
We recapture with the queen, reaching a position similar to lines we’ve seen before. 

Our main idea is to take on d4 with the knight, deflecting the f3-knight.

And if White recaptures with the queen, there's a discovered attack that wins it.

The evaluation here is already -2.1 in Black’s favor.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/6B1/6n1/2NP1N1q/PPP1B.text: This is already mate in 9! Our main ideas: ...Nd4 to deflect the f3-knight and ...Bh2+.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/7q/6n1/2N2NP1/PPPPBP2.text:
White blocks the bishop’s diagonal and prepares Kg2.

This move would stop our queen from accessing h3, prepare to activate the rook along the h-file, and defend against any possible mate threat.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/8/6n1/2N2NPq/PPPPBP2/.text:
That’s why we play 11...Qh3!

This threatens ...Ne5 or ...Nd4 to eliminate the f3-knight — the only defender guarding h2.

Black is totally winning.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/7q/3n4/2N4P/PPPPQPPN.text: We jump in with the knight, forking the queen and the c2-pawn, which cannot be defended!

2kr4/ppp2p1p/2n2n2/7q/5Bb1/2NP1N2/PPP1rP.text:
We unleash an exchange sacrifice!

If White recaptures with the rook, we follow up with ...Bxf3.

Even though we’re down the exchange and a pawn, Black stands better. White’s king is wide open and difficult to defend.

Black has an advantage.

2kr4/ppp2p1p/2nb1n2/6q1/6b1/2NPP1P1/PPP1.text:
And we take the knight. We’re still down a point of material, but our pieces are more active, and our king is significantly safer.

If 14.Rxf6, we should first capture the bishop with tempo on the queen and then take the rook. 

If 14.Bxg4, we simply recapture with the knight.

2krr3/ppp2p1p/2n2n2/6pq/5Pb1/2NPBN2/PPP1.text:
White’s best response is to accept the sacrifice.

We capture the pawn, deflecting the dark-squared bishop from the e-file and reactivating our rook’s threat against e2.

2krr3/ppp2p1p/2n2n2/7q/5Bb1/2NP1N2/PPP1B.text: White regains the pawn, but the light-squared bishop is now under pressure.

2krr3/ppp2p1p/2nb1n2/6Nq/6b1/2NPB1P1/PPP.text:
White accepts the pawn, but this allows us to simplify, and we still remain better.

Taking with the bishop would’ve been worse: after ...Rxe2 and ...Bxf3, Black would have enormous pressure and a -4.5 evaluation.

We start by capturing the dark-squared bishop, which is the only defender of the g5-knight.

2krr3/ppp2p1p/2nb1n2/6pq/6b1/2NPBNP1/PPP.text:
White declines the pawn and develops the rook to e1, adding a defender to the bishop on e2. 

But…

A brilliant bishop sacrifice!

The goal: rip open the center and expose White’s king.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2NPBNP1/PPP1.text:
White acknowledges the threat and develops the bishop to block the rook’s influence on the e-file.

The best move in the position! 

This pawn push invites White to capture, potentially giving up two pieces for a rook and a pawn, and even opens up possibilities for a piece sacrifice to rip open the king’s defenses.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/8/7P/PPPPNPPN/R1.text:
In that case, we keep adding pressure. We’re still a pawn down, but we are miles ahead in development.

12.Nc3 Nb4 is an idea to win c2. This position is definitely not easy for White.

12.Nf3 g5 with the idea of ...g4 is also a great variation for us.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
White plays 6.Nc3, developing with tempo.

This move is played 56% of the time. If we respond correctly, Black wins nearly 60% of games from this position.

We play 6...Qh5!

The queen stays active, adds pressure on f3, and supports future ideas like ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/8/2N2N2/PPPPBP.text:
White develops with 7.Be2, adding a defender to the knight and preparing to castle.

It’s the most natural response in this position.

We stick to our plan, developing the light-squared bishop to its ideal square.

r3k2r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2N2N1P/PPPPB.text:
White plays 9.h3, asking our bishop to decide: trade or retreat?

We choose neither and castle long!

This brings the king to safety, connects the rooks, and sets up possible threats against h2.

Alternatively, 9...Bxh3 is a less ambitious option — sacrificing the bishop with the idea of forcing a draw by threefold repetition.

r3k2r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2N2NP1/PPPPB.text:
White blocks the dark-squared bishop’s diagonal, but weakens the light squares around the king. 

Black now has the initiative and, according to the engine, a clear edge — roughly -1.0.

We stay true to our plan: castling long, bringing the king to safety, and connecting the rooks.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/2N2N2/PPPPBP.text:
White castles with 8.0-0. That's the most popular move, but not the best.

According to the engine, Black has already equalized.

And we continue with our development.

At this point, all our minor pieces and the queen are developed.

We’re fully mobilized and ready to castle long.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3q4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
The knight retreats to f3, getting out of danger. This is the most popular response by White, played nearly 40% of the time.

We continue developing with 5...Nc6.

Yes, we’re still a pawn down, but we already have three pieces out and easy development ahead.

Our plan is simple: play ...Bg4 and long castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White captures again with 4.exd5, opening the center. Around 65% of games include this move. 

We’re now two pawns down, but we’ll recover one immediately and aim to compensate the remaining pawn with piece activity and initiative.

We recapture with the queen, centralizing it and hitting the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White takes on e5 more than 30% of the time. 

But we’re ready to launch...

The Petroff Gotham Gambit!

With 3...d5, which is played in just 1% of games, we challenge White immediately and steer them away from main line theory. 

If White accepts, they remain a pawn up... for now.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight to f3, immediately attacking our e5-pawn.

We enter the Petroff Defense with 2...Nf6 — a direct counter to e4.
Instead of defending, we counterattack. 

This defense appears in around 12% of games.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of Chapter 1 in the Petroff Gotham Gambit.

In this study, we’ll explore lines where White plays 8.0-0, and we respond with an aggressive approach.

White opens with the classic 1.e4, grabbing space and opening lines for development.

We reply symmetrically with 1...e5, staking our own claim to the center.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBP.text:
We follow suit by castling long. 

With opposite-side castling now on the board, we have more active pieces and better development, even if we’re still a pawn down. 

Our next move will likely be 8...Bd6.

If 8.h3, we’ll enter familiar territory from the previous study, and respond with ...Qh5.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/2NP1N1P/PPP.text:
White opens the diagonal for their dark-squared bishop.

We develop our bishop to its ideal square.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/2NPBN2/PPP1.text:
White continues developing, bringing out the dark-squared bishop.

We also develop our bishop, this time to b4, pinning the knight to the king.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/1b4b1/P1NPBN2/1PP.text:
White challenges our bishop.

Instead of retreating, we take the knight and damage White’s queenside pawn structure.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/P1PPBN2/2P1BP.text: White recaptures, accepting the doubled pawns in return for the bishop pair.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3n3q/6b1/P1PPBN2/2P1BP.text:
We improve the knight by jumping to d5, targeting the weak c3-pawn.

Next, we’ll likely bring the h-rook to the center, and can even look for a rook lift with ...Rd6.

2kr3r/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2NPBN1P/PPP1.text:
White brings out their dark-squared bishop as well.

We bring our h-rook to the center, occupying the open file. 

All of our pieces are now developed and active.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/1b4b1/2NPBN1P/PPP.text:
White castles long, taking a different approach to all the other lines we’ve seen in the chapter, but this turns out to be a mistake! 

With precise play, Black can seize the advantage here.

A brilliant queen maneuver! We’ve just hung the bishop, but it’s all part of the plan.

The queen swings to the queenside, increasing the pressure on c3 and preparing either ...Ne4 (thanks to the pinned d-pawn) or ...Nd5.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q7/1b4P1/2NPBN2/PPPQ.text:
White accepts the bishop and is now up four points of material. But things aren’t so simple.

We continue the assault by increasing pressure on c3. White is materially ahead, but their position is crumbling.

Note: 13...Ne4 doesn't work — White can simply take the knight, and after 14...Rxd2 15.Bxd2, they’ll be winning with two pieces and a rook for the queen, plus a pawn advantage.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n5/R7/6P1/2nPBN2/PPP1BPP1.text:
White takes our queen. 

They’re still up four points of material.

However, both of their rooks are available for capture, and choosing the right one can shift the balance in our favor.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n5/R7/6P1/3PBN2/PPP1BPP1/.text:
We choose the d1-rook. If White captures our knight, we simply take the other rook and emerge two exchanges ahead.

If they try to save their rook, we go for ...Nxf2 followed by ...Rxe2 and come out a full exchange up.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n5/q2n3R/1b4P1/2NPBN2/PPP.text:
White tries a creative defensive resource, pinning the d5-knight to our queen. But this allows us to simplify and emerge up an exchange.

We capture the knight on c3 first, hitting the queen.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2n5/q2n3R/6P1/2QPBN2/PPP1B.text:
White recaptures with the queen. 

Capturing with the b-pawn would have been fatal due to ...Qxa2, and the king would be completely exposed.

We take the queen with the knight, which is the only winning continuation for Black.

2krr3/ppp2ppp/2nb1n2/7q/6b1/2NPBN1P/PPPQ.text:
White connects rooks and prepares to castle long.

We pin the knight to the queen, improving the position of our dark-squared bishop and adding pressure to the c3-knight. 

The position is now equal.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/1B5q/8/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
White chooses not to defend the f3-knight and instead develops the bishop to a more active square.

No problem for us as we still develop the bishop to g4. 

We’re not worried about the potential doubled pawns.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
White keeps developing logically, and now the queen must move again, as it's under attack.

We slide the queen over to h5, keeping it active and pressuring the f3-knight. 

This also supports future ideas like ...Bg4 and castling long.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/8/5N2/PPPPBPP.text:
Instead of gaining a tempo on the queen, White opts to quickly develop the light-squared bishop to castle short as soon as possible.

This is a small sideline, with 15% of games going like this.

We stick to our plan and develop the light-squared bishop to g4, increasing pressure on the f3-knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/8/2N2N2/PPPPBP.text:
White plays 7.Be2, reinforcing the knight on f3 and getting ready to castle.

We stick to the plan and activate the light-squared bishop.

r3k2r/p1p2ppp/2pb1n2/7q/6b1/2NP1N2/PPP2P.text:
We develop our bishop and complete minor piece development. 

Despite being down material, the position is equal.

All our minor pieces and the queen are active, we’ll likely castle short soon, and we have two open files to play with.

r3kb1r/p1p2ppp/2p2n2/7q/6b1/2NP1N2/PPP2P.text: White opens the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2B2n2/7q/6b1/2N2N2/PPPP1P.text:
White exchanges bishop for knight, aiming to damage our pawn structure.

We recapture the piece and accept the structural damage.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPP.text: White completes their plan and castles kingside, bringing the king to safety.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/2N2N1P/PPPPB.text:
White asks our bishop a question, but is it really a threat? 

Not quite, since if they take the bishop, we simply capture the hanging rook on h1.

We stick to our plan and castle long. 

Development is nearly complete, and we’re ready to bring every piece into play.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/7q/6b1/2NP1N2/PPP1B.text:
White’s other option is to open up the diagonal for their dark-squared bishop.

We follow our usual plan, castling long.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3q4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
The knight returns to f3, stepping out of danger.

We continue to bring our pieces out. Even though we're still down a pawn, our rapid development puts us ahead on activity.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White accepts the pawn.

We recapture with the queen, centralizing it and placing immediate pressure on the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White grabs the pawn on e5.

This is the Petroff Gotham Gambit!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops the knight and puts pressure on our e5-pawn.

We enter the Petroff Defense, a  symmetrical response that counterattacks e4 rather than defending e5 directly.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
For this second study, we will continue our exploration of the accepted gambit with the retreat 5.Nf3.

We will explore setups with 8.d3 or 8.h3.

White begins with the most common first move, claiming space in the center.

We mirror White’s move.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3qN3/1b1P4/2N5/PPP.text:
Our opponent probably just gave up the pawn on d4, but keeping queens on the board and staying active is in the spirit of our opening.

We will resume play with ...Be6 and ...0-0, and will look for the right time to take on d4, as in: 7.Bd2 Qxd4.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1b1P4/2N5/PPP1QP.text:
Less than 10% of games go like this. White tries the same tempo trick on us, intending to gain time on our king and quickly castle queenside. 

It looks like we will have to play ...Be6 and accept White's plan...

But ...Ne4 works in our favor! The tactics on c3 again prevent White from exploiting the temporary pin.

9.f3 Bxc3+ wins for Black.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1b1P4/2N5/PPPB1P.text:
Black was threatening to take on c3 twice, so White goes for Bd2.

You'll see Bd2 about 78% of the time, and Bb5 10%. 

But both of those moves are mistakes!

Castling deals with the weak king and brings another attacker. White's king is looking very vulnerable now.

For example: 9.a3 Bxc3 and we will continue with ...Re8+. White loses.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q5/8/1b1Pn3/2N5/PPPBQPP.text:
White unpins, again threatening to win our pinned knight.

So we remove an attacker.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q5/8/3Pn3/2B5/PPP1QPPP/.text:
And White recaptures.

We needed to unpin to avoid losing the knight, and castling brings the rook out and tucks the king in a safer spot.

Black's weaknesses are resolved, and White still has problems to fix.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2Bpp/2n2n2/4N3/3P4/8/PPP2PqP.text:
White gets their check.

We will move our king up and stay in contact with the bishop.

This will be important later.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2N2n2/3q4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
This is the most popular way to respond, and it happens 45% of the time.

The point is to trade Black's attacker.

We don't want to ruin the pawn structure unnecessarily, and we step out of tempo moves like Nc3 and c4, so we take with the queen.

Also, notice the pressure on g2, making it harder for the bishop on f1 to move.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3qN3/2BP4/8/PPP2P.text:
21% of the time we see this skewer, as White wants to take f7 with check!

We have to let it happen, but we get the g2-pawn and weaken White's king too.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3qN3/3P4/2N5/PPP2.text: 11% of the time, White tries to run us off the board with Nc3...

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4N3/2BP4/8/PPP2Pq.text:
White's safe option.

But now there's no attack on f7.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
By far the most popular with 56% of the games following this line, White develops the knight with a threat.

Let's go for a clever trick. Instead of making a slow move like ...a6, we use tactics to both defend the threat and prepare to castle.

8.Bb5 will not work.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4P3/2B5/8/PPP2PqP/R.text:
White recaptures, but their pawn isn't safe on e5 in the long- or short-term.

Our active knight will pose some problems. 

We attack h2, and our knight could give a check on f3 later.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1b1P4/2N2Q2/PPP.text:
White has nothing better than Be2 to block the check.
 
Playing Be3 would have allowed ...Bxc3+.

Ne2 might avoid losing pieces, but after Black plays ...Qxc2, White goes down a pawn with the kingside pieces out of play and a lost position.

Removing a defender of e2. 10...Bxc3 is a tempo move that forces white to recapture on c3 or lose a piece.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/2B2Q2/PPP1B.text:
If White ever moves the queen away from f3, we can capture the pawn on g2.

So they recapture with the bishop.

And the stars align!

White can't avoid losing material now.

r1b2b1r/ppp1kBpp/2n2n2/4N3/3P4/8/PPP2PqP.text:
White saves the rook. If they play Nxc6, ...bxc6 is the only move to retain advantage.

Let's remove the defender of the bishop.

r1b2b1r/ppp1kBpp/5n2/4P3/8/8/PPP2PqP/RNB.text:
Not the only way for White to keep material roughly equal, but overwhelmingly the most popular.

We will now pick up material and open up lines for our pieces.

r1b2b1r/ppp2kpp/5P2/8/8/8/PPP2PqP/RNBQKR.text: White's position is so bad that taking back the piece is not the best move, but almost everyone does it anyway.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1b1P4/2N2Q2/PPPB.text:
20% of games continue like this, where White tries to hold onto the material and castle, but that will only make a bad situation worse. 

Of course, we throw in the check on e8!

Not only do we gain time, but we also forcibly lure a piece where alignment with two other targets converges.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1b1P4/2N5/PPPBBP.text:
Be2, giving away the g2-pawn, is the most common attempt at survival, with 38% of players choosing the move.

However, it is losing.

Black finally regains material equality. 

White's activity is illusory.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2q5/8/2QPn3/2B5/PPP2PPP/.text:
White tries to solve both issues and stay up a pawn by trading queens, but this is a mistake! 

Qf3 was the only move for equality.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1b1P4/2N2B1q/PPPBQ.text:
White prepares to castle queenside.

Be3 first is a bit more popular, but mostly just transposes to the same line.

We improve the rook with tempo.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1b1P4/2N2B2/PPPB1P.text:
Defending the rook but opening up the e-file.

The queen might seem a bit oddly placed, but it is actively putting pressure on White, and the g4-square is important for later.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/5q2/8/2QPn3/2B5/PPP2PPP/.text:
And since we aren't on White's team, why should we cooperate?  

White's king is stranded in the center and must make some material concession to escape, so we attack the weak f2-pawn. 

Black is both practically and objectively better despite being a pawn down. The evaluation is -1.6.

12.f3 Qh4+ and White must move the king or lose material.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/4b3/4P1B1/2B3n1/8/PPP2PqP.text:
Black has a powerful position. 

h2 cannot be defended, as our queen can come to e4 with check in case of Bf4 by White.

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/2Q2n2/8/3P2b1/2B5/PPP1BPP.text:
White can still test us, so we mustn't fall asleep. 

Playing ...bxc6 here would blunder everything away!

White would simply have f3.

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1b1P2b1/2N1BB1q/PPP.text:
This is the move that breaks through for us. 

13.Bxg4 Nxg4 and we are converging on the e3-bishop. 

White is completely lost.

r4b1r/ppp2kpp/5P2/8/6b1/8/PPP2PqP/RNBQKR.text:
We can continue to develop with incredible pressure against the white king.

White's position should crumble soon, as the evaluation is -7.5.

r5k1/ppp2ppp/2Q2n2/8/3P2b1/2B5/PPP1rPPP/.text:
Black is better, but can't hold onto the extra piece because of f3 or h3.

Instead, Black will have good chances in the endgame being up a pawn with a good knight vs a bad bishop. 

The evaluation is -2.2.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3qN3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White plays d4, defending the knight and controlling the center.

It's one of the top three choices here at 32%, so we will be seeing it quite often.

We bring the knight out to challenge and pressure the center, and White has to consider that we threaten to win the pawn back. 

Black is winning more than half of their games after ...Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White accepts the gambit, hoping for an easy advantage.

Allowing White a second pawn on d5 would be too generous, so we take it with the most active piece, forcing White to do something about the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White takes the material and challenges us to prove our point.

Normally, we would kick out White's invading knight and then regain our pawn. 

But, instead we offer White a pawn in exchange for development speed and the initiative!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
Challenging the dark squares.

Instead of defending, we counterattack!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
This chapter is all about White defending their knight with 5.d4. 

In this study, we will look at how to maximize our initiative after 6.Nxc6 and 7.Nc3, and also to respond after the less common 6.Bxc4 and 6.Nc3.

White begins with 1.e4.

So we claim the dark squares in similar fashion.

4r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1BPP2b1/8/PP2NPqP/R2.text:
White has no way to save the knight here.

Since Black's king is safe and our pieces are active and coordinated, while the opposite is true for White, Black is clearly better.

The evaluation is -4.2.

Although piece trades will happen, we don't necessarily need to force them as all the pressure is on the White king.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1bPP4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Keeping the c1-bishop flexible is the only good way to defend here.

Let's bring the rook to the party, while the introverted king takes the opportunity to find a corner away from the action.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1bPP4/8/PP1B1PPP.text:
What seems like a natural move, counterattacking the undefended bishop on b4, is a mistake!

It looks like we are hanging our bishop, but the White king is critically weak, and their dark-squared bishop was an important defender.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2qb1n2/8/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black's lead in development lets us retain the initiative for the pawn, and Black is scoring a very respectable 57% win rate here. 

The consistent theme in this position is control of the e-file and weakening White's dark squares with moves like ...Bg4, provoking f3, ...Nd5 or ...Ng4 to trade the bishop on e3, or ...c5 to break White's chain in the future. 

We could also consider trading off White's better light-square bishop, but our specific plans must be adjusted based on what White chooses to do.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2N2n2/3q4/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
White tries to hold onto all their advantages by trading off the weak knight on e5 for the attacker.

Taking with the queen keeps the pawn structure intact.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
While c4 is joint second in popularity with c3 at just 10%, they are quite different approaches to our main lines from White, and thus worth understanding.

With c4, White tries to dominate the center with pawns.

If we were to develop slowly or passively, White would simply be a pawn up. 

Our bishop check will help speed up our development.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/2P5/PP3PPP/.text: This is obviously an attempt to be solid and unambitious, just holding onto the pawn, and 10% of games go this way.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/4B3/PPP2PPP.text:
In most of our lines, White is actively fighting for control of the light squares, and has major trouble with the e-file in particular. 

Here, White tries to fix the e-file problem first. 

It takes a 5% share of games from here, with Black still winning 53%.

So, naturally, we take the light squares and develop a bishop.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/8/PPP1QPPP/.text:
And finally, for this study, let's look at the most aggressive responses. 

7.a4 with the threat of Bb5 can be neutralized by ...a6, so we can set that aside.

Qe2 is down to 4% of games from here, and White is doing much better, losing half of their games and winning 44%... but still good for us!

This odd-looking move is once again about using the e-file, without delay!

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/3P4/1bP5/2N1B3/PP.text:
Using the correct bishop to block the file.

It's time to save our queen, and we centralize on an active square.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/3P4/1bP5/2N5/PP2B.text:
White may think that they can move the f1-bishop now that the attack on the g2-pawn is blocked...

But that would be a mistake.

White hung c4, and we can remove the defender of e2 and weaken the pawn structure.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/3P4/2P5/2P5/P3BPP.text:
White has taken back immediately in every game, but it doesn't help with c4 undefended. 

Kf1 would have been a better choice!

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1BPP4/8/PP1K1PP.text: Let's have a quick look at Kd2 trying to hide on the queenside.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1BPP4/8/PP2BPPP.text:
Let's look at the optimistic attempt first. White blocks with the bishop.

But that left the g2-pawn hanging! And now we are attacking the rook.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2q5/8/1BPPn3/8/PP1K1PPP.text:
Black will equalize material at the very least, with a safer king and better pieces. The evaluation is -3.

Trading off White's biggest asset, the bishop pair, would further emphasize the advantage.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/3q1n2/3P4/1bP5/2N1B3/PP.text:
White is up a pawn and looks like they are getting everything they want, but not so fast!

We threaten to liquidate all of White's advantages if they castle.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/3q4/3P4/1bP1n3/2N1B3/PP.text:
So White defends the weak c3-square.

Our previous plan was stopped, but it has layers. We develop our last minor piece to the most active square.

We are actually threatening to capture on c3 now.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3P4/2q5/2P5/P3BPPP/.text:
So we take the pawn. The bishop on e2 is loose, the pawns on d5 and c3 are hanging, and White's king is unable to castle. Although material is equal, and White has the bishop pair, Black is much better, with the evaluation showing -4.6.

Black should continue to play actively against White's king to make the most of the position while picking up the odd pawn if possible.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1BPP4/8/PP2BPqP/R.text:
White saves the rook, but their king will never feel safe again.

...Bg4 works because we first removed the g2-pawn.

If White plays f3 now we can just take the pawn.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/3P4/1bP5/2N5/PP3PP.text:
White finally deals with the pressure on g2, and with tempo.

But we have a stronger threat before moving the queen, and actively tie down White's pieces with pins.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1BPP4/8/PP3PPP/R.text:
We are now down a bishop and a pawn, but that is only part of the story. 

We are ready to bring all of our pieces into the attack.

It's time to bring the pain to White. 

They have three ways to defend, and none of them are good.

r1bk1b1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/3P4/2N5/PPP1QPP.text:
White controls important light squares and prepares to castle queenside.

And of course we should pin the knight!

We will create threats on both the e-file and c3, and one dark-squared bishop can't cover both.

r1bk3r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1bQP4/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
White tries to force us to trade down with nothing for our pawn.

Before we deal with that, let's give a check and grab the e-file.

r1bkr3/p1p2ppp/2p5/3n4/1b1P4/2N1B3/PPPK1.text:
White moves the king to d2, and the two weakest squares in White's camp are defended.

We aren't without resources, though. We fight for the light squares that White can't control.

r1bkr3/ppp2ppp/2Q5/3n4/1b1P4/2N1B3/PPP2P.text:
White should just trade the queens off.

Forced.

r1bkr3/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/8/1bQP4/2N1B3/PPP2P.text:
Of course, White had a plan and is about to castle.

But not so fast! We have this sneaky move using the pin on the knight and defending the bishop. 

10...Nd5 will complicate things again, although in reality, should White castle, we are mainly just threatening to win our pawn back on c3 and play on with equal material. 

...Nxe3 is also playable.

r2kr3/p1p2ppp/1np1b3/8/3P4/P1P1B3/2PK1PP.text:
See how we have locked down outposts in front of the white king?

Even though White is better here according to the engine, we can still force concessions and play a good game, as White's advantage is mostly just material.

r2kr3/p1p2ppp/2p1b3/3n4/1b1P4/P1N1B3/1PP.text:
White will probably want to unpin their knight at some point, so they attack our bishop.

And if so, we just take.

r3k2r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/5b2/1b1P4/2N1B3/PPP2.text:
You should be getting used to the pin idea by now. 

Black is winning 64% of games here. 

Objectively the engine calls it equal, but practically it is just difficult for White to do anything here and we will regain our pawn.

We will look to centralize the knight on f6. We are also flexible to castle on either side of the board.

r3kb1r/ppp2ppp/2q2n2/5b2/3P4/2N1B3/PPP2P.text:
Half of the time White brings the knight out.

We were threatening to win our pawn back on c2 and leave White with a weak pawn on d4.

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/3q4/3P1b2/1bP1n3/2N1B3/PP.text:
And when White does castle...

We launch our hidden plan.

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/3q4/3P1b2/1bP5/2P1B3/P3BP.text: Of course White wants to keep the rook...

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/3q4/3P1b2/2P5/b1P1B3/P3BP.text:
But the rook is trapped! If Ra1, then ...Bb2.

Black only has a minimal edge here, since even if we win the exchange, White would have the bishop pair and a strong extra central pawn.

r3r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1BPP2b1/2N5/PP2BPqP.text:
Bringing the inactive knight out to defend the bishop.

We sacrifice the rook! 

We want to bring the other rook to e8 and we don't give White any time to fix anything this way.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3qN3/3P4/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
White guards the knight and prepares to bring out the rest of their pieces.

We will build tension in the center, not allowing White time to get comfortable.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White takes a second pawn, accepting the gambit.

Taking with the queen gains a tempo on the knight and pressures g2 for now.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White takes the pawn, with some pressure on the weak f7-square too.

Let's go for our gambit. More decisions for White to think about.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
And White challenges.

We will counter-challenge and give White a decision to make.

Take some material or defend?

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
In this second study in the 5.d4 chapter, we will look at a few sidelines White might also play after 6.Nxc6 Qxc6.

Let's begin!

"Best by test" according to Bobby Fischer is 1.e4.

We will contest it with 1...e5.

N2q1k1r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/5b2/5B2/8/PPP1QPPP.text:
We immediately target the knight. 

If White tries to retreat with 13.Nc7, then 13...Nd4 is crushing, forking the queen and the c2 pawn. 

Black is already better.

r1b1k2r/pppNbppp/8/3n4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB1.text: White keeps simplifying with another trade.

r1b1k2r/pppnbppp/5n2/3QN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:

r1bq1rk1/2p1bppp/2p2n2/p7/8/1PN5/PBPPQPP.text:
We start pushing the a-pawn, aiming to open lines against the enemy king. White's queen is still blocking their bishop in. 

The idea of ...Bc5–Bd4 was also available to counter the bishop on b2.

That said, White holds a clear advantage. The engine gives +1.7, but this line is rare, and still presents White with many practical problems.

r1bq1rk1/p1p1bppp/2p2n2/8/8/1PN5/PBPPQPP.text: White castles long and achieves a safe king with well-placed pieces.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2N2n2/8/8/1PN5/PBPPQPP.text:
White captures our knight, damaging our structure, but opening the b-file in the process.

We recapture.

r1bqk2r/ppN1bppp/2n2n2/8/5B2/8/PPP1QPPP/.text:
Here it comes: 11.Nc7+ forks our king and rook. 

At first glance, it looks like White will win material and keep the knight safe, but…

We calmly slide the king to f8.

r3k2r/pppbbppp/8/3n4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB1KB.text:
We take back with the bishop.

Our plan is to castle long, play ...Bc6, and look for active knight jumps like ...Nf4 or ...Nb4.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/1N2N3/3q4/8/PPP1QPP.text:
White jumps in with the knight, forking our queen and the c7-pawn, which would also fork our king and rook.

We retreat the queen to its original square, covering c7.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/1Q1qN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White can also go for the immediate queen trade. It’s the second-best option for White, but it only shows up in about 6% of games.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/3qN3/2P5/8/PP1PQPPP.text:
White pushes the c-pawn to hit our queen and prepare a strong center.

This is the second most played move at the amateur level, but it’s already inaccurate. Black has equalized.

White players choose this move 13% of the time.

We sidestep to a5, keeping the queen active and pinning the d-pawn to the king.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/3qN3/8/2N5/PPPPQPPP.text:
White develops while gaining a tempo on our queen. It's the best and most popular move here, played in 64% of games.

We go back to d8. We sidestep any Qb5+ ideas that could force a queen trade.

The upside? White’s queen is awkwardly placed on e2, and we’ll soon generate activity. In nearly every variation except one, we’ll have clear compensation for the pawn.

rnb1k2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/q3N3/2P5/2N5/PP1PQP.text:
White develops and breaks the pin, now preparing d4 to claim the center.

We castle short. 

Our plan is simple: bring the rook to e8, line it up with the queen, and develop the knight to c6.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3qN3/8/8/PPPPQPPP/R.text:
This is White’s best response to the gambit, as mentioned in the introduction, though it only shows up in 22% of games.

It threatens a discovered check and forces us to be precise.

We acknowledge the threat and develop our dark-squared bishop, blocking the queen’s vision along the e-file.

rnb1r1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/q3N3/1bPP4/2N5/PP1B.text:
And now we pin the other knight, this time to the queen! 

Thanks to our better piece activity and the awkward placement of White’s queen, we’re already pressing for an advantage. Our next move will likely be ...Nc6.

If White ever moves the queen off the e-file, ...c5 becomes very strong, should we have tempo to achieve it.

rnb2rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/q3N3/2PP4/2N5/PP2QP.text:
White gains central space, but now the c3-knight is pinned to the king.

We improve our bishop and add pressure to the pinned knight on c3.

rnb2rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/q3N3/1bPP4/2N5/PP1BQ.text: White breaks the pin by developing the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/1PN5/PBPPQPP.text:
White fianchettos their bishop, preparing to castle long.

They’re catching up in development with a safe king.

We develop our knight, inviting the trade. We actually want White to double our pawns, as it opens lines on the queenside.

Other ideas included ...Bc5–Bd4 to challenge the fianchettoed bishop, or simply pushing our queenside pawns with ...a5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/2N3P1/PPPPQP.text:
White completes the fianchetto, developing the bishop toward the long diagonal.

We place our rook on the open e-file, lining it up directly with White’s queen.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/2NP4/PPP1QPP.text:
We castle short. 

Our ideas are clear: place the rook on the e-file, pin the knight on c3, and develop with ...Nc6.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2N2n2/1N6/5B2/8/PPP1QPPP.text:
White sacrifices the knight on c6 to open the bishop’s diagonal and support the idea of jumping into c7 with check.

We recapture with our knight.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/1N2N3/5B2/8/PPP1QPP.text:
White develops the bishop and x-rays the c7-pawn. If the e5-knight ever moves, c7 will be attacked twice.

So we push ...c6, kicking the knight back and preventing tactical problems on c7.

Our plan is simple: castle short for safety, and if White brings a rook to the d-file, our queen will escape to a5.

But let's also see a line that looks dangerous, yet gives us an advantage.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/3P4/2N5/PPP1QPP.text:
This is the second most played move, played in 19% of games, but it simply hangs a pawn!

We gladly take the pawn back. Material is now equal.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/1PN5/P1PPQPPP.text:
This is the best option for White and the only line that keeps the +1 advantage.

It has appeared in just 3% of amateur games, but was played in the only known master-level encounter.

The idea is to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop along the long diagonal and prepare long castling.

We castle short. 

Since White will likely castle long, we're aiming to create imbalances.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/2N3P1/PPPPQP1.text:
White prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and aims to castle short. 

This setup is played in 13% of games, but it gives Black an easy path to equalize.

We castle short.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/2NP4/PPP1QPPP.text:
White opens their dark-squared bishop. 

At the amateur level, this move is seen about 34% of the time.

And already, Black is nearly equal here.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3PN3/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
White accepts the gambit.

We recapture with the queen, activating it and putting pressure on the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
White captures the pawn on e5.

And now we’re in the Petroff Gotham Gambit!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
White develops a knight and immediately targets our e5 pawn.

We go for the Petroff Defense, a mirrored setup that challenges e4 right away instead of defending e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the study of Chapter 3 in the Petroff Gotham Gambit.

In this one, we’ll explore what happens after 5.Qe2, which is White’s strongest reply against our gambit.

White opens with the most popular first move, staking a claim in the center.

We respond symmetrically.

rnbqr1k1/ppp1bppp/5n2/4N3/8/2N3P1/PPPPQP.text: White brings their king to safety.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2b1N3/8/2N3P1/PPPPQ.text:
And now comes our idea! By playing ...Bc5, we threaten ...Bd4, which would win a piece.

White’s best option is to play d4, giving up a pawn in order to allow their dark-squared bishop to defend the e5-knight.

2kr1b1r/pppb1ppp/8/3p4/2PPn2q/3B4/PP3PPP.text:
We castle long and look to develop our bishop to d6. 

If White tries to prevent that with c5, we’ll change plans and look to fianchetto the bishop with ...g6 and ...Bg7.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3q4/8/2NN4/PPPP1P.text:
White develops their other knight and gains a tempo by hitting our queen.

We keep the queen active by staying on the fifth rank.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q7/8/2NN4/PPPPBPP.text:
The knight on d3 is so awkwardly placed that the engine already suggests moving it again.

Instead of addressing the misplaced piece, White develops the light-squared bishop and prepares to castle short.

We jump forward with the knight, improving the piece and threatening to win the bishop pair, even if it’s not immediately possible. 

Another option was ...Bd6, an equally strong move, but ours is the less common choice.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/q7/3n4/2NN4/PPPPBPP.text: White gets the king to safety.

r1bq1b1r/pppn1kpp/8/3p3Q/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
White brings the queen into the attack, but it’s not as threatening as it looks.

Playing 7...g6 would be a mistake.

It allows Qxd5, losing the central pawn for no reason.

r1bq1b1r/pppn2pp/4k3/3p3Q/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
The king steps up to defend the d5-pawn. 

The position is equal. 

Our next move will be ...Ndf6, reinforcing our center. 

White may try to force a perpetual check, but if they go for a passive move like 0-0, we’ll already be better.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p5/2npP3/8/8/PPP1BPPP/R.text:
We solidify our center with ...c6.

Our next steps will be to finish our development with ...Be7, castle short, and likely place our light-squared bishop on f5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/2npP3/8/8/PPP1BPPP/RN.text: White retreats the bishop, preserving the bishop pair.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/4n3/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
White recaptures.

We retreat the knight to c5, targeting the light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppN1ppp/8/3p4/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
White trades knights.

We recapture with the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1Npp/8/3p4/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
White sacrifices the knight, but there’s no real danger.
